hero.filename: Chalmette National Park and Fazendeville, Louisiana, aerial view from southwest, 1963.jpg
hero.caption: This 1963 U.S. Government photo provides an aerial view of the historic African American village of Fazendeville, Louisiana in relation to the Chalmette National Historic Park and Battlefield, including the Chalmette Monument. The village was razed during the mid-1960s to facilitate expansion of the national park (public domain photo maintained by the Open Parks Network, Clemson University).

images.filename: Fazendeville, Louisiana (front of State of Louisiana historical marker, Chalmette National Battlefield entrance, St. Bernard Highway).jpg
images.caption: Public domain photo of the front of the State of Louisiana historical marker commemorating the former, historic, African American village of Fazendeville in St. Bernard Parish, Louisiana, which was razed during the 1960s to facilitate the expansion of the Chalmette National Historic Park and Battlefield. Funds for the marker were provided by the St. Bernard Tourist Commission and the St. Bernard Parish Office of Tourism and Film. The marker, which is located at the national battlefield's entrance on St. Bernard Highway was dedicated in a special ceremony on April 19, 2021. (Note: Additional text related to Fazendeville's history inscribed on back of marker.)

images.caption: "Building a Future of Freedom. After the Civil War, former slaves built a thriving town on the battlefield at Chalmette. They bought the land from a free man of color, Jean Pierre Fazende. In 1966, the National Park Service acquired the land to preserve the battlefield. Fazendeville’s people moved to other places, but they are still a community at heart." (Trading card from Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve in Louisiana)
